notes.text: And — In Mount Zion, in God's church. All people - Both Jews and Gentiles. A feast - A feast made up of the most delicate provisions, which is manifestly meant of the ordinances, graces, and comforts given by God in his church. Of wines - Which have continued upon the lees a competent time, whereby they gain strength, and are afterwards drawn off, and refined.
The face — The covering of the face. The veil - The ignorance of God, and of the true religion, which then was upon the Gentiles, and now is upon the Jews.

He — Christ will by his death destroy the power of death, take away the sting of the first death, and prevent the second. In victory - Hebrew. unto victory; so as to overcome it perfectly; which complete victory Christ hath already purchased for, and will in due time actually confer upon his people. Rebuke - The reproach and contempt cast upon his faithful people by the ungodly world.
Our God — Our Messiah, long since promised, and for whom we have waited long, is come into the world, bringing salvation with him.
Judah — Or Israel, one tribe being put for all. Judah he mentions as the chief of all the tribes.
The mountains — Horeb and Sinai, two tops of one mountain, and other neighbouring mountains.

Tremble — The mountains did more than what was fit at the appearance of the great God. We are to give glory to God, not to ourselves or idols, ver. 1-8. By trusting in his promise and blessing, ver. 9-15. And by praising him, ver. 16-18.

glossa.text:
*At the going out.* ((AUG.)) Here things past are not related, but things to come are foretold, because in those deeds things to come were signified: and therefore not all the things which were done there are spoken of here, but certain of them otherwise, lest he be thought to be recounting things past. ((CASS.)) First the Prophet tells what wonders God gave to the Hebrews in figure, and to Christians in spirit. Secondly he asks why these things were done, there, *What ailed thee, O sea?* Thirdly he reproves the empty idols of the Gentiles, and commends the religion of God, there, *the idols of the Gentiles.*

*At the going out.* As it were, when Israel, that is, the house of Jacob, went out of Egypt, that is, from a barbarous people.

 *Barbarous.* ((AUG.)) That tongue is barbarous which praises not God.
*It was made.* ((CASS.)) As that people, when it went out of Egypt, etc., *as far as* they are able to resist vices, and this.

*The sea saw,* that is, the sinners of the world. *Jordan,* they who by divers desires snatch men into the great sea, that is, into the embittering malice of this world; but these things cease at the coming of the Lord, being as it were turned backward.

*The sea saw.* ((AUG.)) This is here said otherwise than it was done. There it is read to have stood on that side from which the waters were flowing down, nor is anything said there of the mountains skipping; but both the things done there and the things said here are figures.

*Rams.* ((ID.)) Who with the horns of both, etc., *as far as* every knowledge lifting itself up against Christ. *The hills.* ((CASS.)) From tilling, the middling sort: for these things are not according to the letter; whence also by the sea and by Jordan, that is, by the ancient deeds, doubt not that those things are signified which today are done spiritually.
*What ailed thee.* ((ID.)) Secondly he asks why these things were, that he may stir up wonder. And he resolves it: *At the face of the Lord.*

*At the face.* ((ID.)) One answer for two, because one author both made the ages to be astonished, and made his own, that is, the mountains and the hills, to rejoice: for at the appearing of Christ men were moved from their own superstition to the worship of God.

*At the face of the God of Jacob.* And as though one should ask, who is the Lord? The God of Jacob, not a new one; who makes them wrestle.

*Who turned the rock.* ((ID.)) The hard hearts of the Jews, unto the water of baptism.

*The crag.* The Gentiles, that they also may pour forth the watering fountains of preaching.

((AUG.)) That is, himself, hard before, while he was not known, etc., *as far as* he might overflow upon all that believe, saying: *If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.*
*The house of Israel.* ((CASS.)) Here he shows the profit of the Christian religion.
*The house of Aaron.* ((AUG.)) But lest that should seem to be already a thing possessed by the greater which to the lesser is a hope, he adds, *The house of Aaron.*
*Mindful.* ((CASS.)) That he might convert them, and he blessed the converted through the same.

*Upon you.* ((AUG.)) Because the number of teachers increased.

*Upon the children.* Because the number of followers also increased. Therefore ye both, fathers and sons, are blessed of the Lord, who made you *heaven* in the greater, *and earth* in the lesser; or who made every creature.

*Blessed be ye of the Lord.* ((CASS.)) He who above wished to be blessed, now with confidence says, *Blessed,* which belongs to God, that ye may serve him. Truly *of the Lord,* because even *the heaven of heaven,* that is, Christ, is unto the honour of the Lord; or,

*The heaven of heaven,* that is, the empyrean, he gave to the Lord Christ, according as he is man. *But the earth.* This lower earth he gave. *To the children of men.* That in it they may purify themselves; or the people to the preachers; whence: As the Father hath sent me, and I will send you ((Joan. VI)).

*The heaven of heaven.* ((AUG.)) He speaks of those whose minds, etc., *as far as* whom the weak cannot yet see without a support.
*Nor all they that go down.* ((CASS.)) Or, not all they that go down; because the saints also went down, but not into the lower place.

notes.text: Your glorying — Either in your gifts or prosperity, at such a time as this, is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven - One sin, or one sinner. Leaveneth the whole lump - Diffuses guilt and infection through the whole congregation.

Purge out therefore the old leaven — Both of sinners and of sin. That ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened - That is, that being unleavened ye may be a new lump, holy unto the Lord. For our passover is slain for us - The Jewish passover, about the time of which this epistle was wrote, ver. 11, was only a type of this. What exquisite skill both here and everywhere conducts the zeal of the inspired writer! How surprising a transition is here, and yet how perfectly natural! The apostle, speaking of the incestuous criminal, slides into his darling topic, - crucified saviour. Who would have expected it on such an occasion. Yet, when it is thus brought in, who does not see and admire both the propriety of the subject, and the delicacy of its introduction?

Therefore let us keep the feast — Let us feed on him by faith. Here is a plain allusion to the Lord's supper, which was instituted in the room of the passover. Not with the old leaven - Of heathenism or Judaism. Malignity is stubbornness in evil. Sincerity and truth seem to be put here for the whole of true, inward religion.

glossa.text: *The whole lump.* They were partakers, in that they suffered the guilty man. But if anyone has not the power to cast out one whom he knows to be guilty, or is not able to prove it, he is free from blame. And it is not the judge's part to condemn without an accuser, as neither did Christ cast out Judas.

*Paste.* It is flour kneaded together with water without leaven, that is, unleavened bread. He wills therefore that these be some one thing through love, pure from the corruption of sin, having put on the new man, as they were made in baptism. Zyma in Greek, fermentum in Latin.

The Pasch is an immolation, not a passing over, as to certain men it seems, for first the Pasch and so the passing over: because first is the example of the Saviour, and so salvation.

((AUG.)) This renewal of our life is a certain passing over from death to life, etc., *as far as* since Christ our pasch is immolated.
*Of sincerity.* Of the new life and of truth, without any deceit, that sincerity may make life clean, and may exclude every deceit of truth.

notes.text: Mark xvi, 12.
Today is the third day — The day he should have risen again, if at all.
O foolish — Not understanding the designs and works of God: And slow of heart - Unready to believe what the prophets have so largely spoken.

Ought not Christ — If he would redeem man, and fulfil the prophecies concerning him, to have suffered these things? - These very sufferings which occasion your doubts, are the proofs of his being the Messiah. And to enter into his glory - Which could be done no other way.
He made as though he would go farther — Walking forward, as if he was going on; and he would have done it, had they not pressed him to stay.
They constrained him — By their importunate entreaties.
He took the bread, and blessed, and brake — Just in the same manner as when he instituted his last supper.
Their eyes were opened — That is, the supernatural cloud was removed: And he vanished - Went away insensibly.
Did not our heart burn within us — Did not we feel an unusual warmth of love! Was not our heart burning, &c.
The same hour — Late as it was.

The Lord hath appeared to Simon — Before he was seen of the twelve apostles, 1 Cor. xv, 5. He had, in his wonderful condescension and grace, taken an opportunity on the former part of that day (though where, or in what manner, is not recorded) to show himself to Peter, that he might early relieve his distresses and fears, on account of having so shamefully denied his Master.
In the breaking of bread — The Lord's Supper.
Jesus stood in the midst of them — It was just as easy to his Divine power to open a door undiscernibly, as it was to come in at a door opened by some other hand. Mark xvi, 14, 19; John xx, 19.
He showed them his hands and his feet — That they might either see or feel the prints of the nails.
While they believed not for joy — They did in some sense believe: otherwise they would not have rejoiced. But their excess of joy prevented a clear, rational belief.
He took it and ate before them — Not that he had any need of food; but to give them still further evidence.

And he said — On the day of his ascension. In the law, and the prophets, and the Psalms - The prophecies as well as types, relating to the Messiah, are contained either in the books of Moses (usually called the law) in the Psalms, or in the writings of the prophets; little being said directly concerning him in the historical books.

Then opened he their understanding, to understand the Scriptures — He had explained them before to the two as they went to Emmaus. But still they understood them not, till he took off the veil from their hearts, by the illumination of his Spirit.

Beginning at Jerusalem — This was appointed most graciously and wisely: graciously, as it encouraged the, greatest sinners to repent, when they saw that even the murderers of Christ were not excepted from mercy: and wisely, as hereby Christianity was more abundantly attested; the facts being published first on the very spot where they happened.
Behold I send the promise — Emphatically so called; the Holy Ghost.

glossa.text: *Named Emmaus.* Emmaus is itself the metropolis, a notable city of Palestine, which, after the storming of Judea, was restored under the prince Marcus Aurelius Antonius, and changed its name along with its condition.

*While they talked together.* The Lord draws near and accompanies them as they speak of him, that he may both kindle in their minds the faith of the resurrection, and fulfil what he had promised he would do: *Where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them ((Matth. XXVIII))*. *Drawing near,* etc. *Their eyes,* etc. He appeared indeed in his own form, but did not show the form which they might recognize. As they both loved him within and yet doubted, so he himself is present outside and at hand, and does not show who he is. To those who speak of him, then, he grants his presence; but from those who doubt of him he takes away the appearance by which he might be known.

*Art thou a stranger,* etc. *To whom,* etc. They think him a stranger whom they do not recognize. And truly he was a stranger to them, from whose frailty he now stood far off through the glory of the resurrection, and from whose faith, ignorant of the resurrection, he remained an alien. *A man, a prophet,* etc. *And how they delivered him up,* etc. They confess him a prophet and a great one; of the Son of God they are silent, either because they do not yet believe perfectly, or, if they believe, they fear to be delivered into the hands of the Jews, not knowing with whom they speak.

*But we hoped,* etc. In a manner they refute themselves, in that they had hoped for redemption in him whom they had seen dead, nor did they believe that he would rise again; and they grieve most of all that he was slain without guilt, whom they had known to be innocent; and from this they were walking sorrowful .

*They affrighted us,* etc. They are rightly said *teruisse* those to whom they added more sadness about the body not found than they bring gladness, by the resurrection announced, wherewith they might be refreshed.

*Some of us went,* etc. Since above he said that Peter ran to the monument, and now Cleophas says: *Some of us went to the monument,* etc., it is to be understood that two went together. But he mentioned Peter alone first, because Mary announced it to him first.

*O foolish and slow of heart.* Here a twofold necessity of being humbled presses upon us, who are neither taught in the Scriptures as much as we ought, nor as intent as is fitting on fulfilling the things we know. For if Moses and the prophets spoke of Christ, and had foretold that he would enter through passion into glory, how does he glory that he is a Christian who neither searches out in the Scriptures how they pertain to Christ, nor desires to reach through sufferings the glory which he wishes to have with Christ?

*And he himself,* etc. *Stay with us,* etc. He showed himself such in body as he was among them in mind. They were to be tested, whether they would love at least as a stranger him whom they did not yet love as God. But because they cannot be strangers to the brightness, they with whom the Truth was walking call him to lodging, nay compel him. From which example it is gathered that strangers are not only to be invited to lodging, but even to be drawn in.

*He broke it,* etc. Him whom they did not know in the exposition of Scripture they knew in the breaking of bread; because not the hearers of the law but the doers shall be justified, and the truth is better understood by working than by hearing.
*Their eyes were opened,* etc. The appearance of weakness is withdrawn from the eyes of the flesh, that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds.

*And they said,* etc. Mystically: for this reason another likeness was shown them in Christ, that they might not know him save in the breaking of bread; so that all may understand that they do not recognize Christ unless they become partakers of his body, that is, of the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of the bread, saying: *We being many are one bread, one body ((I Cor. X))*. When therefore he reaches out the blessed bread, their eyes are opened that they may know him, and the impediment is removed which was upon their eyes from Satan, that Jesus might not be recognized. And this impediment the Lord allows to remain until the sacrament of the bread be come to. But when the unity of the body has been shared, the enemy's impediment is taken away, that Christ may be recognized.

*Burning. ((GREG.))* When the word had been heard, the heart, before cold with the numbness of unbelief and of fear, was kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it now burns with a heavenly desire and stretches itself out to believe the truth. By as many precepts as a man is instructed, by so many torches, as it were, is he set aflame.

*The Lord is risen.* Already there was a report that Jesus had risen, made by those women and by Simon Peter, to whom he had appeared; these two found them speaking of these things. But they themselves also had heard earlier that he had risen; yet they feared to say it on the way, when they said only that angels had been seen by the women. For, not knowing him with whom they were speaking, they could fear that they might fall into the hands of the Jews, if they should say anything anywhere about Christ's resurrection.

*Jesus stood,* etc. This appearance is that of which John says ((Joan. XX)): *When it was late that day,* etc., *and he said to them: Peace be to you.* But as to John's saying that Thomas was not with them, while Luke says that these two found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, it is to be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared to them as they spoke of these things.

*To see a spirit. And he said to them.* The disciples had known him to be true man, but after he died they do not believe that true flesh could rise from the sepulchre on the third day. They think therefore that they see the spirit which he sent forth in the passion; but the Lord takes away this error.

*Why are you troubled. ((AMBR.))* The apostles believed, but nevertheless they are troubled, etc., *as far as* that the Lord, with the doors shut, poured himself in unforeseen with his body.

*Thoughts,* etc. False ones, not descending from above, but rising up in the heart like an evil weed. I require the faith which I planted in you; what has sprung from yourselves I condemn. If there is no truth of the resurrection, the fruit of the passion is lost.

*Handle and see.* By many proofs he persuades them of the resurrection, offering himself both to be seen by their eyes and to be handled by their hands; and while by their handling he shows bones and flesh, he marks the state of his own resurrection and of ours, in which our body will be both subtle through the effect of a spiritual power, and palpable through the truth of its nature. After the resurrection the Lord showed in his body two contrary things: both what is palpable, of the same nature, that he might form them to faith, and what is incorruptible, of another glory, that he might invite them to the reward.

*He showed them his hands,* etc. That by showing the scar of his wounds he might heal the wound of unbelief; which scars he both kept then and will keep in the judgment. First, to establish faith in the resurrection; then, that, entreating the Father for us, he may always show what kind of death he endured for man; thirdly, that he may intimate to those redeemed by his death how mercifully they have been helped, by setting before them the tokens of that same death. But lastly, that in the judgment he may declare how justly the impious are condemned, by showing the scar which he received from them. Not therefore from any inability to heal them did he keep the scars, but that he might carry about the perpetual triumph of his victory.

*Have you here anything.* To convey the truth of the resurrection, he willed not only to be touched but to eat with them; not that either he or we after the resurrection ought to need food, but that he might make manifest that he was a body, not a spirit; he ate by power, not by necessity. In one way the thirsting earth soaks up water, in another the hot ray of the sun: the former by need, the latter by power.

*Of a broiled fish.* The broiled fish is the Mediator himself who suffered, taken in the waters of the human race by the snare of death, broiled at the time of the passion. He is also to us a honeycomb in the resurrection. The honeycomb in the wax, that is, the Godhead in the manhood. In the eating of this honey it is signified that he receives into his body, unto eternal rest, those who, when they feel tribulations for God, do not withdraw from the love of the inward sweetness. They who are broiled here shall there be filled with the true sweetness.

*And when he had eaten.* He takes away all evasions : he was seen, he was touched, he ate; and lest in anything he should seem to have deluded the human senses, he puts his hands to the Scriptures, so that even if it should seem, as the pagans say, that by magic arts he was able to do what he willed, they may at least see that he could not have prophesied before he was born.

*Then he opened.* After the sight, after the touch, after the law recalled to mind, he opened their understanding, that they might understand what they see and read; then, after the truth of his own body had been commended, he commends the unity of the Church: *And that there should be preached in his name.*

*It behoved,* etc. It behoved that the ministers who were to preach penance and remission unto all nations should begin from Jerusalem. Not only because to them were entrusted the oracles of God, and because theirs is the adoption of sons, and the glory the testaments, and the law-giving; but for this reason also, that the Gentiles, entangled in various errors and crimes, might by this token above all of the divine loving-kindness be roused to the hope of pardon: that he grants pardon to those who crucified the Son of God.

*But stay you.* After he had perfectly instructed the disciples about the power of preaching, although he could of a sudden, if he willed, have strengthened them, he put it off, saying: *But stay you.* That he might give an example to those who follow, lest the imperfect presume to preach before the time. He sits in the city who binds himself within the cloisters of the mind, lest by speaking he wander abroad outside; so that when he has been perfectly clothed with the divine power, then he may go forth as it were out of himself, by instructing others.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The day is far spent, and the road has been long.
Stay with us, Lord; the evening is near.
A stranger walked with us and opened the Scriptures.
And our hearts burned within us.
He took the bread, blessed and broke it, and we knew him.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us worship the Lord made known in the breaking of bread.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come in off the road as the light goes long and gold, road-weary, heavy with all you cannot explain.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
A stranger fell into step beside you and turned the old story over until your chest went warm.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Then he sat at your table, took the loaf, and broke it — and you saw the marks, and you knew.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
On the mountain God spreads a feast and swallows up death forever; come and taste it now.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Evening falls; the road has worn us thin.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He opens the Scriptures, and our hearts catch fire.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He breaks the bread, and our eyes are opened.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us know him at the table.
We have seen the Lord. Alleluia!
